column4: The section’s dictionary root و ز ر connects the burden removed in 94:2 with a human helper who carries for another; Moses asks, “وَزِيرًا مِّنْ أَهْلِي,” explicitly naming that supporting role.
The section develops Moses’ request for a family helper, and this ayah says Aaron was made “وَزِيرًا” alongside him; it shows the requested burden-sharing role put into place.

The section’s root note links وِزْر to a load that made the back creak; this ayah pictures people “أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ” carrying burdens on their backs, a judgment scene that reverses the relief of 94:2–3.
The section describes God removing the addressee’s load; here the messenger “يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ” and their shackles, a parallel image of a divinely sent helper relieving people’s burden.
The section’s dictionary root و ز ر includes a mountain refuge, while this ayah answers the search for escape with “لَا وَزَرَ” (no refuge); it gives the named shelter a stark limit at judgment.
The section ends by turning toward the Rabb; this ayah says “إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ” is the destination that day, joining refuge to the return to one’s Lord.
The section’s general dictionary gloss for و ز ر is anything one seeks refuge in; here the earth narrows and they realize “أَن لَّا مَلْجَأَ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِلَّا إِلَيْهِ,” making God the sole refuge.
The section ends with the addressee’s turning to the Rabb; this command, “فَفِرُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ,” makes that movement an urgent flight toward God.

The section says its root’s broad refuge sense covers what one hides in or fortifies oneself with; the speaker says no one can protect him from God and “وَلَن أَجِدَ مِن دُونِهِ مُلْتَحَدًا,” ruling out refuge elsewhere.
The section’s dictionary explicitly calls the root و ز ر a mountain one flees to for refuge; Noah’s son says “سَآوِي إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍ يَعْصِمُنِي مِنَ الْمَاءِ,” but the mountain cannot save him.

The section defines ظَهِير as a helper, as if one back rested against another; this ayah calls the angels “ظَهِيرٌ” for the Prophet after naming Allah his protector, while the wives’ mutual backing had opposed him.

The section’s root note presents a backer as support for a master and ends by turning to the true Rabb; this ayah says the disbeliever is “عَلَىٰ رَبِّهِ ظَهِيرًا,” a reversal in which support is set against one’s Lord.
The section’s dictionary root ظ ه ر names a helper or backer; after the killing, Moses vows “فَلَنْ أَكُونَ ظَهِيرًا لِّلْمُجْرِمِينَ,” setting a moral boundary on whom he will support.

The section links a helper with the back as a place of support; Moses asks “اشْدُدْ بِهِ أَزْرِي.” The section explicitly notes that أَزْرِي is a different root from و ز ر, while the bodily image still meets the helper who strengthens him.
The section develops a helper who shares another’s task; Moses asks Pharaoh to send Aaron as “رِدْءًا يُصَدِّقُنِي,” a support who can stand with and confirm him.
The section’s helper leans in to strengthen another; God answers Moses, “سَنَشُدُّ عَضُدَكَ بِأَخِيكَ,” promising strength through his brother.

The section links an opened chest and an eased task with Moses’ request for Aaron; in this parallel prayer his chest narrows and he asks, “فَأَرْسِلْ إِلَىٰ هَارُونَ,” showing the helper answers a constricted speaker’s need.

The section’s helper and refuge images meet in this plea from the oppressed: they ask God to appoint “وَلِيًّا” and “نَصِيرًا” from Himself, making protection and support a response to people who cannot release themselves.
The section notes that Moses’ plea for a helper follows his request for an opened chest; he begins “رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي,” the same need for inward opening before a difficult task.
The section places Moses’ request for a vizier beside his request for ease; “وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي” states the task-relief that the helper is meant to make possible.
The section quotes Moses asking for a family vizier in 20:29; this next ayah names “هَارُونَ أَخِي,” identifying the brother who will carry the supporting role.
After asking for Aaron and strength in 20:29–31, Moses asks “وَأَشْرِكْهُ فِي أَمْرِي”; this ayah’s contribution is shared work, not only borrowed strength.
The section says Moses’ helper is requested so they can glorify God; this next part of the same prayer gives that purpose as “كَيْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيرًا.”
Continuing the purpose in 20:33, this ayah says “وَنَذْكُرَكَ كَثِيرًا”; shared support serves abundant remembrance as well as glorification.
After Moses’ requests for a helper, shared work, and remembrance in 20:29–34, God answers “قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ”; this neighbor completes the image by showing the plea granted.
The section’s minister is a helper who carries another’s work; Moses tells Aaron “اخْلُفْنِي فِي قَوْمِي” and to set things right, showing Aaron entrusted to stand in for him during his absence.

The section’s root note for ظ ه ر treats backing as support; this ayah condemns people who “تَظَاهَرُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِالْإِثْمِ وَالْعُدْوَانِ,” so mutual support can add wrongdoing rather than lift a burden.
The section develops a backer as someone who stands with another; here people “ظَاهَرُوا عَلَىٰ إِخْرَاجِكُمْ” by aiding your expulsion, a hostile use of support that marks its boundary.
The section identifies Rabb as the obeyed master and directs the addressee to the Rabb; Pharaoh’s claim “أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ” is the opposing, false claim to that authority.
The section’s dictionary defines ر ب ب as owner and obeyed master as well as Lord; Joseph calls the household owner “رَبِّي” when refusing to betray him, illustrating the human-master sense.
The section names ر ب ب as master and owner; in Joseph’s prison interpretation one servant “فَيَسْقِي رَبَّهُ خَمْرًا,” using the word for an earthly master.
The section’s human-master sense of ر ب ب appears when Joseph asks the released servant “اذْكُرْنِي عِندَ رَبِّكَ”; the servant is to appeal to the king who holds authority over him.

The section echoes “to your Rabb” as the destination of turning; Joseph is told “ارْجِعْ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ” about the women, where Rabb means the earthly king, clarifying the master sense beside the divine address.

The section defines Rabb as owner and obeyed master while directing the reader to God; this call rejects taking one another as “أَرْبَابًا مِّن دُونِ اللَّهِ,” setting a limit on human claims to that authority.
The section’s root ر ب ب includes the obeyed master; this ayah says people took their scholars and monks as “أَرْبَابًا مِّن دُونِ اللَّهِ,” a concrete warning against misplaced obedience.

The section’s dictionary root و ز ر describes one bearer taking a load off another; this ayah says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى,” limiting that image when the load is each soul’s moral liability.

The section’s root و ز ر names a burden, but here “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى” says moral guilt is not transferred from one soul to another; relief from one’s load has a personal-accountability boundary.

The section describes a helper carrying a burden off someone; this ayah says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى” and that even a heavily laden soul’s plea brings none of its burden onto another, a direct limit on human load-sharing.

The section joins a removed وِزْر to turning toward the Rabb; this ayah says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى” and later “ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُم مَّرْجِعُكُمْ,” pairing personal responsibility with return to the Lord.
The section’s root note connects وِزْر with a carried load; the ayah states “أَلَّا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى,” the boundary that no one carries another’s guilt.
The burden rule in 53:38 continues here: “وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَى” says each person has only what they strove for, clarifying the personal load that cannot be shifted.
Continuing the personal-accountability statement of 53:38–39, this ayah says “وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ”; each person’s own striving is made visible before its recompense.

After 53:38’s no-transfer rule and the next two ayat on each person’s striving, this neighbor says “ثُمَّ يُجْزَاهُ الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَىٰ,” completing the account of an individual’s burden and result.

The section’s dictionary root و ز ر pictures a helper taking a load away; this ayah says misleaders bear “مِنْ أَوْزَارِ الَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَهُمْ,” an opposite case where leading others astray adds to one’s own burden.

The section’s helper bears another’s weight to relieve him; this ayah says the misleaders carry “أَثْقَالًا مَّعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ,” showing that sharing another’s burden can instead increase it when one leads them astray.

This ayah names turning away from God’s reminder; its next neighbor, 20:101, calls the consequence a load borne on Judgment Day, contrasting the relieved burden with one accumulated by rejecting remembrance.
Following 20:100’s turning away from the reminder, this ayah says “وَسَاءَ لَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ حِمْلًا,” a burden carried at judgment rather than one removed by God.

The section presents God taking a burden off the addressee; this closing plea asks “وَلَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِ,” making the need for divine release from an unbearable load explicit.

The section’s dictionary gloss for و ز ر includes both a mountain refuge and anything one fortifies oneself with; this ayah says God made “أَكْنَانًا” in mountains and protective “سَرَابِيلَ,” joining shelter and bodily protection in one provision.
Like the section’s addressee receiving relief and a place to turn, the earlier address says God found him an orphan and “فَآوَىٰ” (gave shelter), a direct scene of divine refuge.

The section’s dictionary root note broadens refuge to whatever one seeks shelter and protection in; these youths “أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ” and pray to their Lord for mercy, a concrete sanctuary scene.

The section names the refuge sense of the root و ز ر; these people would rush toward any “مَلْجَأٍ” or cave (“مَغَارَاتٍ”) they could find, showing the flight to an earthly shelter that contrasts with the section’s turn to God.

The section’s lexicon calls a mountain a refuge one flees to; this ayah says death reaches people “فِي بُرُوجٍ مُّشَيَّدَةٍ” (fortified towers), marking the limit of physical fortifications as refuge.
The section’s broad refuge gloss concerns what one fortifies oneself with; this ayah likens false protectors taken besides God to a spider’s house, making an apparent shelter’s weakness visible.

The section links a burden’s release to refuge in the Rabb; here the person asks “أَيْنَ الْمَفَرُّ,” and the next ayah 75:11 answers that there is no refuge, so this row contributes the search that prompts the answer.

The section’s dictionary explicitly links ittizār, wearing a waist-wrap, to و ز ر; this ayah describes clothing that covers nakedness and adorns people, a concrete garment parallel for that secondary sense, though it does not use the word izār.

The section recalls Moses asking for his chest to be opened; this ayah describes God expanding a person’s chest toward Islam and, in contrast, making it tight and constricted, extending the same bodily image to guidance and resistance.

The section connects Moses’ request for an opened chest with a difficult task; this ayah depicts a person whose chest God opens to Islam and who is then on light from his Lord, a direct parallel for the image of inward opening.

The section quotes Moses asking God to open his chest for his mission; this ayah uses the same chest-opening wording for someone who opens their breast to disbelief, showing the image’s contrary direction.

The section’s dictionary describes a vizier as one whose judgment a ruler relies on; here the Prophet is told to consult the believers in a matter and then rely on God when resolved, giving a direct scene of leadership using counsel before turning to God.

The section’s minister is a person relied on for judgment; this ayah describes believers conducting their affairs by consultation among themselves, a collective form of the counsel relation developed in the dictionary note.

The section brings together a helper and the final turn to the Rabb, and also describes angels as supporters; here believers call their Lord for help and He answers by reinforcing them with a thousand angels, joining divine response and angelic support in one scene.
Following the angelic reinforcement in 8:9, this ayah says the angels are reassurance for believers’ hearts and that victory comes only from God; it clarifies the support’s source and purpose.

The section describes angels as supporters and the final appeal to the Rabb; this ayah asks whether it is enough that their Lord reinforce them with three thousand angels, a direct parallel of help sent by the Lord.
Continuing the reinforcement in 3:124, this ayah promises five thousand angels if the believers are patient and mindful; it adds the stated condition for the Lord’s support.

The section’s dictionary says a person’s “back” can mean their supporters; this ayah pictures successive guardians before and behind a person, protecting them by God’s command. The link is an indirect protection scene rather than shared wording.

The section’s dictionary broadens refuge to whatever one seeks shelter and protection in; these youths are told to take refuge in the cave, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease for their affair, combining sanctuary with divine relief.

The section joins a refuge with a supporter who steadies another; in this cave scene the Prophet reassures his companion that God is with them, and God sends down tranquility and unseen aid, meeting both parts of the image.

The section ends by directing the addressee toward the Rabb as refuge; Pharaoh’s wife asks her Lord for a home near Him and deliverance from Pharaoh and his deeds, a concrete flight from an earthly ruler to divine shelter.
The section depicts God removing a load from the addressee; Job calls to his Lord from affliction and says that harm has touched him, identifying the plea whose answer in 21:84 removes it.
Answering Job’s affliction in 21:83, this ayah says God responded and removed his harm, a direct parallel to the burden being taken away.
The section images the Rabb relieving a servant’s burden; in this repeated account Job calls his Lord because Satan has touched him with exhaustion and suffering, a specific plea under a load.
Following Job’s plea in 38:41, this ayah gives him a spring and cold drink by God’s command, showing the practical relief that answers the affliction.
After the relief in 38:42, this neighbor says God restored Job’s family and more as mercy and reminder; it completes the account of the Lord’s response to the burden described in 38:41.
The section’s refuge image ends in turning to the Rabb; Jonah calls to God from darkness, admitting his wrong, which is a concrete appeal from distress toward the only refuge.
Answering Jonah’s call in 21:87, this ayah says God rescued him from distress and does likewise for believers, directly joining appeal to God with release from a burden.

The section’s lexicon gives Rabb the secondary gloss “one who sets things right”; Shuaib says he seeks reform as far as he can, that his success is only through God, and that he relies on and turns to Him, concretely linking reform with dependence on God.
